claims.title: How can a prime avoid every prescribed place and still split the quadratic field?
claims.hypotheses: A positive integer d and a bound B are given. For its geometric application, the integral trace lattice gives the fixed denominator and the automorphic evaluation gives a finite exceptional set.
claims.statement: A prime larger than B and 2d admits a square root of −d in its local integers. It can avoid all tested residue characteristics, the support of the chosen form and the denominators of an evaluation point.

claims.title: How can one tell whether two test places choose the same quadratic root?
claims.hypotheses: An integral generator of a quadratic field has trace t, norm n and discriminant Δ. The prime q avoids Δ and the quadratic polynomial has a residue root.
claims.statement: A prime over q is classified on this quadratic field by the root that is the residue of the generator. For any integral y in that field, Δy has integer coordinates in the generator basis. Conjugation interchanges the two sides.

claims.title: How deep must a level be to fix the chosen automorphic form?
claims.hypotheses: A finite adelic similitude comparison is given with its lattice coordinates and its prime-p kernel, together with a nonzero form transforming under an open level by a character of open kernel at the type place. Its support avoids p.
claims.statement: One depth at a finite set of places ensures that a level-one element satisfying the local congruences has a lift whose inverse transpose belongs to the level of the form and has trivial type character.

claims.title: One integer level for all the prescribed places
claims.hypotheses: Use the stabilizer data, free test places over good primes different from p, and a prescribed positive divisor c coprime to p. Test places above a common rational prime agree on the quadratic subfield.
claims.statement: There is one integer level ≥3 divisible by c and every test prime and coprime to p. Its principal subgroup and the appropriate site subgroup at each test place stabilize the form. Each site ideal is prime to the tested place and retains the depths elsewhere.

claims.title: How can a Hecke trace detect a prescribed system of eigenvalues?
claims.hypotheses: Use the odd-rank group and type, transport of its common eigenvector, and the local idempotent, auxiliary convolution functions and regular-support results at an admissible level.
claims.statement: One test function and one polynomial multiplier detect every word polynomial with nonzero prescribed scalar evaluation. On the selected generalized eigenspace the definite trace is the scalar evaluation times a fixed nonzero power trace.

claims.title: How does one level carry all the requested spectral tests?
claims.hypotheses: The odd-rank unitary representation, its type at w₀, field assumptions and disjoint finite test sets meet the stated spherical, real-place separation and quadratic restriction hypotheses. claims.statement: One level and one system of operators give the weight and good-reduction tests on H, polynomial congruences on C, and polynomial congruences at the remaining eligible spherical places off ℓ outside a finite set. The selected coefficients give a monic polynomial with roots equal to the twisted normalized Satake parameters.

claims.title: Which places must be tested on the same geometric tower?
claims.hypotheses: The type place and the base weight place lie above ℓ, are separate over the real subfield, and agree on the imaginary quadratic subfield. Extra spherical places satisfy the conditions stated separately above and away from ℓ.
claims.statement: Every level choice retains the weight test at the base weight place. An extra eligible place away from ℓ receives a polynomial test on the same level. At a further compatible place above ℓ, separate constructions give the weight test and the polynomial test.

claims.title: How do the field labels determine the base of the tower?
claims.hypotheses: The arithmetic datum has one field label and comes with a field isomorphism η from its coefficient field to E. Its integral element has the specified quadratic trace and norm.
claims.statement: The root η(ω) and the restriction of η to the integers give a standard base. Both label conditions required for the Hodge comparison follow from these equalities.
